nodes.content: Develop unsupervised speech recognition accent adaptation that separates pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation without sacrificing existing accents.
requirements: Reduce unseen-accent word error rate ≥15% relative to frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech.
Limit existing-accent WER increases to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels.

nodes.content: Train accent-gated phoneme residual adapters from confidence-filtered pseudo-labels with adversarial speaker/channel disentanglement and frozen-recognizer fallback for existing accents.
Does a 0.85 pseudo-label confidence cutoff discard systematic vowel shifts needed to train accent-gated phoneme residuals?
A 0.85 cutoff excludes ≥40% of shifted-vowel frames; phoneme-balanced inclusion down to 0.70 should reduce unseen-accent WER.
Compare 0.85 filtering with phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling on unlabeled AccentShift-12, measuring shifted-vowel retention and speaker/channel-stratified unseen/existing-accent WER.
Train AccentShift-12 adapters with 0.85 filtering versus phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling; audit shifted-vowel retention and speaker/channel-stratified WER.
On AccentShift-12, 0.85 filtering excluded 44% of shifted-vowel frames; balanced 0.70 sampling lowered unseen-accent WER from 28.0% to 24.1%.
Provisionally prefer phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling over 0.85 filtering for its 3.9-point WER gain; verify frozen-baseline and existing-accent constraints.
Benchmark provisionally selected balanced-0.70 adapters against frozen ASR, independently crossing held-out speakers and channels to test both WER constraints.
AccentShift-12 benchmark report tabulating frozen versus balanced-0.70 WER across unseen/existing accents and independently crossed speaker/channel conditions.
Ablate speaker/channel adversaries under both AccentShift-12 sampling policies; measure nuisance-probe accuracy and crossed-speaker/channel WER.
Adversaries reduced balanced-0.70 existing-accent WER from 13.4% to 12.6% across independently crossed speakers/channels; frozen scored 11.0%.
Add speaker/channel-invariant accent-novelty gating to balanced-0.70 adapters, routing low-novelty utterances to frozen ASR to protect existing accents.
Calibrate speaker/channel-invariant novelty on unlabeled adaptation and existing-accent speech; route familiar utterances to frozen ASR, then audit crossed-speaker/channel WER.
Calibrate novelty gate at the existing-accent 95th percentile using unlabeled audio; compare routed WER against n8's crossed-condition frozen baselines.
AccentShift-12 gate-calibration report recording the 95th-percentile novelty threshold, routing rates, and crossed-condition WER against frozen baselines.
Does the 95th-percentile novelty threshold route too many unseen-accent utterances to frozen ASR to achieve 15% relative WER reduction?
At the 95th-percentile gate, ≥85% unseen-accent adapter routing should yield ≥15% relative WER reduction without >1-point existing-accent regression.
Evaluate n13’s 95th-percentile gate on AccentShift-12: measure unseen-accent adapter routing, frozen-relative WER, and crossed-condition existing-accent WER change.
On AccentShift-12, 87% of unseen-accent utterances reached adapters; WER fell 29.0%→24.3% (16.2% relative), while crossed-condition existing-accent WER rose 11.0%→11.5%.
Stress-test the 95th-percentile gate across held-out AccentShift-12 speaker/channel pairs; measure unseen-accent routing, frozen-relative WER, and existing-accent regressions.
On held-out mobile-channel speakers, unseen-accent routing was 68%, WER fell 30.0%→27.0%, and existing-accent WER rose 11.0%→12.3%.
Channel-normalized phoneme-shift gating should yield ≥85% mobile unseen-accent routing, ≥15% frozen-relative WER reduction, and ≤1-point existing-accent regression.
Retest the original 95th-percentile gate on held-out far-field and headset cohorts, logging unseen-accent routing, frozen-relative WER, and existing-accent regression.
On held-out far-field/headset cohorts, unseen-accent routing reached 86%; WER fell 28.0%→23.4% (16.4% relative), while existing-accent WER rose 11.0%→11.6%.
Fit a channel-normalized phoneme-shift gate on unlabeled speech; measure mobile unseen-accent routing, frozen-relative WER, and crossed-condition existing-accent WER.
On crossed mobile-speaker/channel conditions, normalized gating routed 88% of unseen-accent utterances; WER fell 30.0%→25.2%, but existing-accent WER rose 11.0%→12.2%.
Sweep channel-normalized gate thresholds on crossed mobile-speaker/channel cohorts; chart unseen-accent WER reduction against worst-cohort existing-accent WER regression.
At the 97th-percentile threshold, mobile routing reached 86%; WER fell 30.0%→25.4% (15.3% relative), while worst-cohort existing-accent WER rose 11.0%→11.9%.
Select 97th-percentile channel-normalized gating: unlike the initial 1.2-point regression, it limits regression to 0.9 points with 15.3% relative WER improvement.
Train a phoneme-level adapter router on augmentation-consistent pronunciation shifts; revert speaker/channel-sensitive routing decisions to frozen decoding.
Does augmentation-consistency gating wrongly reject shifted consonants under mobile compression, eroding unseen-accent WER gains?
Compression-aware consistency training should retain ≥80% of shifted-consonant segments on mobile audio while keeping unseen-accent WER ≤25.5%.
Compare standard versus compression-aware consistency routers on AccentShift-12 mobile audio; audit shifted-consonant retention and frozen-relative unseen-accent WER.
Train standard and compression-aware consistency routers using unlabeled AccentShift-12 audio; score mobile shifted-consonant retention and unseen-accent WER.
On mobile AccentShift-12, compression-aware routing retained 83% shifted consonants versus 69% standard; unseen-accent WER was 25.3% versus 26.6%.
Test compression-aware routing on held-out mobile codecs crossed with unseen speakers; measure shifted-consonant retention and unseen-accent WER.
On held-out Opus mobile codecs and unseen speakers, compression-aware routing retained 74% shifted consonants and produced 26.1% unseen-accent WER.
Codec-randomized articulatory-feature consistency should restore ≥80% shifted-consonant retention and ≤25.5% unseen-accent WER on held-out Opus speaker crosses.
Randomize training codecs and enforce articulatory-feature consistency; test held-out Opus consonant retention, unseen-accent WER, and existing-accent regression.
Train codec-randomized articulatory routers without Opus audio; evaluate shifted-consonant retention and unseen-accent WER on held-out Opus speaker crosses.
Held-out Opus speaker crosses retained 82% shifted consonants with codec-randomized articulatory routing; unseen-accent WER fell from 26.1% to 25.2%.
Provisionally select codec-randomized routing: initial mobile success failed on Opus, but retention recovered 74%→82% and WER 26.1%→25.2%; audit existing accents.
Benchmark codec-randomized routing against frozen ASR on AccentShift-12 speaker/channel crosses; report unseen-accent relative WER reduction and worst existing-accent regression.
AccentShift-12 codec-router audit table comparing frozen and adapted WER per accent across independent speaker/channel crosses, with worst existing-accent regression.
Infer accent-specific pronunciation variants from unlabeled ASR lattices, marginalizing speaker/channel embeddings and preserving frozen decoding for familiar variants.
Mine unlabeled AccentShift-12 lattices for nuisance-marginalized pronunciation variants; gate variants against frozen decoding and audit crossed speaker/channel WER.
Extract top-20 phoneme paths per unlabeled utterance; cluster variant alignments after speaker/channel embedding subtraction and estimate accent-specific pronunciation weights.
AccentShift-12 variant lexicon containing weighted phoneme alternatives, cluster support counts, and speaker/channel-adjusted lattice scores for gated decoding.
What fraction of lexicon variants recur across independent speaker/channel cells rather than arising from lattice word-substitution errors?
Requiring variants in ≥3 independent speaker/channel cells should retain ≥70% genuine accent shifts while rejecting ≥60% word-substitution errors.
Manually audit 300 held-out AccentShift-12 lexicon variants; measure genuine-shift retention and substitution-error rejection under ≥3-cell speaker/channel support.
In the 300-variant audit, ≥3-cell support retained 74% of genuine accent shifts and rejected 63% of lattice word-substitution errors.
Annotate 300 held-out Opus/headset lexicon variants across crossed speakers; measure ≥3-cell genuine-shift retention and substitution-error rejection.
On 300 held-out Opus/headset variants, ≥3-cell support retained only 61% of genuine shifts, despite rejecting 66% of substitutions.
Codec-stratified two-cell support plus articulatory agreement should retain ≥70% genuine Opus/headset shifts while rejecting ≥60% substitutions.
Partition variant evidence by codec, require two independent speaker/channel cells and matching articulatory shifts, then audit substitutions and genuine variants.
Apply codec-stratified two-cell articulatory filtering to 300 held-out Opus/headset variants; score genuine-shift retention and substitution rejection.
On 300 held-out Opus/headset variants, codec-stratified two-cell filtering retained 73% genuine shifts and rejected 62% substitutions.
Blind-audit 300 new Opus/headset variants across disjoint speakers, comparing two-cell articulatory filtering with three-cell support on retention and rejection.
On 300 disjoint-speaker Opus/headset variants, two-cell filtering retained 75% genuine shifts but rejected only 54% substitutions.
Defer two-cell filtering for decoding: substitution rejection fell from 62% to 54% on disjoint speakers; strengthen error controls.
Adding bidirectional lattice agreement to deferred two-cell filtering should retain ≥70% genuine shifts and reject ≥60% substitutions on disjoint speakers.
Add bidirectional lattice agreement to codec-stratified two-cell filtering; audit genuine-shift retention and substitution rejection on disjoint-speaker Opus/headset variants.
Ablate bidirectional lattice agreement in two-cell filtering on disjoint-speaker Opus/headset variants; score genuine-shift retention and substitution rejection.
On a new disjoint-speaker Opus/headset audit, two-cell filtering without bidirectional lattice agreement retained 72% genuine shifts and rejected 61% substitutions.
Apply bidirectional lattice agreement to two-cell Opus/headset variants from disjoint speakers; quantify genuine-shift retention and substitution rejection.
On the same disjoint-speaker Opus/headset audit, bidirectional agreement rejected 74% of substitutions but retained only 66% of genuine shifts.
Defer lexicon decoding: bidirectional agreement retains only 66% of genuine shifts, while two-cell substitution rejection varies 54%–61% across audits.
Annotate 600 held-out lexicon variants; report cross-cell recurrence and substitution-error fractions across independent speakers, channels, and codecs without decoding.
AccentShift-12 variant-audit dataset with 600 labeled candidates, speaker/channel/codec recurrence counts, and genuine-shift versus substitution-error tags.
Train pronunciation-prototype adapters on unlabeled accent speech with speaker/channel-swapped views and worst-cell frozen-logit constraints on existing accents.
Does worst-cell frozen-logit regularization suppress genuine pronunciation prototypes while protecting existing accents across speaker/channel crosses?
Familiar-prototype-only frozen-logit KL should preserve ≥80% shifted-phoneme coverage, ≥15% unseen-accent WER reduction, and ≤1-point worst-cell existing-accent WER regression.
Compare uniform versus familiar-prototype-only KL on unlabeled AccentShift-12; audit shifted-phoneme coverage and frozen-relative WER across speaker/channel crosses.
Reproduce n41's codec-router audit; compare uniform versus familiar-only KL on shifted-phoneme coverage and frozen-relative unseen/worst-existing WER.
On AccentShift-12, familiar-only KL covered 83% of shifted phonemes; unseen WER fell 30.0%→25.2%, while worst-cell existing WER rose 11.0%→11.8%.
Compare uniform and familiar-only KL with n41's codec-router audit on disjoint far-field/headset speakers; score shifted-phoneme coverage and unseen/worst-existing WER.
Disjoint far-field/headset speakers: familiar-only KL covered 76% shifted phonemes; unseen WER fell 28.0%→24.2% (13.6% relative).
Downweight KL for swap-stable shifted prototypes to achieve ≥80% coverage, ≥15% unseen-WER reduction, and ≤1-point existing-WER regression on far-field/headset crosses.
Estimate prototype stability under speaker/channel swaps; relax KL only for stable shifts, then audit coverage and crossed-condition WER.
Benchmark swap-stability-weighted KL against n41's codec-router audit on disjoint far-field/headset speakers; measure shifted-phoneme coverage and unseen/existing WER.
On disjoint far-field/headset speakers, swap-weighted KL covered 82% shifted phonemes; unseen WER fell 28.0%→23.6%, existing worst-cell WER rose 11.0%→11.8%.
Audit swap-weighted KL against n66's 600 labeled variants; measure genuine-shift coverage, substitution uptake, and far-field/headset crossed-condition WER.
Against n66, swap-weighted KL covered 81% genuine shifts and admitted 8% substitutions; unseen WER fell 28.0%→23.7%, worst-existing WER rose 11.0%→11.8%.
Select swap-weighted KL over familiar-only KL: disjoint-speaker coverage recovered 76%→82%, unseen WER 24.2%→23.6%, existing regression stayed 0.8 points.
Validate selected swap-weighted KL on untouched AccentShift-12 speaker/channel crosses; measure shifted-phoneme coverage, frozen-relative unseen WER, and worst-cell existing regression.
AccentShift-12 validation report with untouched speaker/channel-cross WER by accent, shifted-phoneme coverage, and frozen-baseline comparisons for swap-weighted KL.
